prompt: All sounds are made by objects that are doing what?
hints: Touch your throat while you hum. What do you feel?
solution: All sounds are made by **vibrating** objects: things moving quickly back and forth, like a guitar string or your vocal cords.

prompt: What is the unit of frequency? (Give the name or the symbol.)
hints: It's named after the scientist Heinrich Hertz.
solution: Frequency is measured in **hertz (Hz)**: the number of vibrations (waves) per second.

prompt: Light travels in [[a]] lines. When light reflects off a mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of [[b]].
hints: Shadows have sharp edges because of the way light travels.
solution: Light travels in **straight** lines. The law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of **reflection**.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: How high or low a sound is
The number of vibrations per second
The material a wave travels through

hints: Amplitude is linked to loudness; frequency is linked to pitch.
solution: Pitch → how high or low; amplitude → size of the vibration; frequency → vibrations per second; medium → what the wave travels through.

prompt: Why can't sound travel through outer space?

options.text: Space is a vacuum, so there are no particles to pass on the vibrations
Space is too cold for sound
Sound travels too slowly to cross space
The Sun's light blocks the sound

feedback.b: Temperature isn't the reason. Sound needs particles.
feedback.c: Speed isn't the problem. Sound can't travel there at all.
feedback.d: Light doesn't block sound.

hints: What does sound need in order to travel?
solution: Sound is passed on by particles vibrating. Space is a **vacuum**, with no particles, so sound can't travel through it. Light can, because it doesn't need a medium.

prompt: The traces show three sounds on the same settings. Which sound has the **highest pitch**?

figure.alt: Three sound wave traces on the same scales. A: two waves across the screen, small height. B: four waves across the screen, the same small height. C: two waves across the screen, about twice as tall as A.

options.text: A
B
C
They all have the same pitch

feedback.a: A has only two waves across the screen, so it has a low frequency.
feedback.c: C has the tallest waves, which makes it the loudest, not the highest pitch.
feedback.d: B has twice as many waves across the screen as A and C.

hints: Pitch depends on frequency. Which trace has the most waves across the screen?
solution: **B** has the most waves in the same time, so it has the highest **frequency**, and that means the highest pitch.

prompt: Look at the same three traces. Which sound is the **loudest**?

figure.alt: Three sound wave traces on the same scales. A: two waves across the screen, small height. B: four waves across the screen, the same small height. C: two waves across the screen, about twice as tall as A.

options.text: A
B
C
They are all equally loud

feedback.a: A's waves are short (small amplitude), so it's quiet.
feedback.b: B has the highest pitch, but its waves are no taller than A's.
feedback.d: C's waves are clearly taller than the others.

hints: Loudness depends on amplitude, the height of the wave.
solution: **C** has the tallest waves (biggest **amplitude**), so it is the loudest. It has the same pitch as A.

prompt: White light is split by a prism into a spectrum. Put the colours in order, starting with red.
hints: Remember the name "ROY G BIV".
solution: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (**ROY G BIV**), the same order as in a rainbow.

prompt: A ray of light hits a mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
hints: Use the law of reflection.
solution: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = **35°** (both measured from the normal).

prompt: Why does a red apple look red in white light?

options.text: It reflects red light and absorbs the other colours
It absorbs red light and reflects the other colours
It gives out its own red light
It turns white light into red light

feedback.b: We see the colour that is reflected into our eyes, not the colour that is absorbed.
feedback.c: An apple isn't luminous. It doesn't make its own light.
feedback.d: The apple doesn't change light into a new colour. It reflects one colour and absorbs the rest.

hints: White light contains all the colours. Which one reaches your eye from the apple?
solution: White light contains all colours. The apple **reflects red** light into your eyes and **absorbs** the other colours, so it looks red.

prompt: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface. What causes this?

options.text: Refraction: light changes speed and direction as it passes from water into air
Reflection: light bounces off the water's surface
The water really bends the straw
Light travels in curved lines through water

feedback.b: Reflection happens too, but the bent look comes from light changing direction as it leaves the water.
feedback.c: Take the straw out and it's still straight.
feedback.d: Light travels in straight lines inside the water. It changes direction only at the boundary.

hints: Light travels at a different speed in water than in air.
solution: Light from the straw under the water **refracts** (changes speed and direction) as it passes from water into air. Your brain assumes the light travelled in a straight line, so the underwater part looks out of place.

prompt: Select **all** the things that sound can travel through.

options.text: Air
Water
Steel
Wood
A vacuum
Outer space

hints: Sound needs particles to pass on the vibrations.
solution: Sound travels through **solids, liquids and gases** (air, water, steel, wood). It can't travel through a vacuum, and outer space is almost a perfect vacuum.

prompt: During a storm, Hemi sees a flash of lightning and hears the thunder 3 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far away is the lightning? (Assume the light arrives instantly.)
hints: The sound took 3 s to reach Hemi.
Distance = speed × time.
solution: $d = v \times t = 340 \times 3 = 1020$ m, about 1 km away.

prompt: Put these in order of the speed of sound through them, from **slowest** to **fastest**.
hints: Sound travels faster when the particles are closer together.
solution: Air (about 340 m/s) → water (about 1,500 m/s) → steel (about 5,000 m/s or more). The particles are closest together in solids.

prompt: When white light passes through a glass prism, it spreads out into a spectrum of colours. Why?

options.text: Each colour refracts by a different amount, so the colours separate
The prism adds colours to the white light
The glass reflects each colour off a different face
The prism absorbs the white and lets the colours through

feedback.b: The colours were already in the white light. The prism only separates them.
feedback.c: The light passes through the prism. It's refraction, not reflection, that spreads it out.
feedback.d: White light is made of the colours. There's no separate "white" to absorb.

hints: White light is a mixture of colours. Do they all bend by the same amount?
solution: White light is a mixture of colours. Each colour **refracts** (bends) by a slightly different amount in glass (violet the most, red the least), so they spread out into a **spectrum**.

prompt: On stage, a performer in a red T-shirt is lit only by a **blue** spotlight. What colour does the T-shirt look?

options.text: Black
Red
Blue
Purple

feedback.b: To look red it must reflect red light, and there is no red light here.
feedback.c: A red T-shirt absorbs blue light rather than reflecting it.
feedback.d: Colours of light don't mix on the T-shirt like paint. It can only reflect red, and there is none.

hints: A red object reflects red light only. Which colours are in the spotlight?
solution: The red T-shirt can only reflect **red** light, but the spotlight gives only **blue** light, which the T-shirt absorbs. No light is reflected, so it looks **black**.

prompt: Tama shouts towards a cliff and hears the echo 2 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff?
hints: An echo is sound that has travelled to the cliff **and back**.
Find the total distance travelled, then halve it.
solution: Total distance the sound travelled: $340 \times 2 = 680$ m. That's there and back, so the cliff is $680 \div 2 = 340$ m away.

prompt: Explain how the sound from a guitar string reaches your ear and lets you hear it.
modelAnswer: When the string is plucked, it vibrates back and forth. The vibrating string pushes on the air particles next to it, making them vibrate too. Each particle passes the vibration on to the next, so the sound travels through the air (the medium) as a wave, while the particles themselves only move back and forth. When the vibrations reach your ear, they make your eardrum vibrate, and you hear the sound.

rubric.criterion: The string vibrates (moves quickly back and forth)
The vibrations are passed through the air (medium) from particle to particle as a sound wave
The vibrations make the eardrum vibrate

hints: Start with the string. What is it doing?
How does the vibration get across the room?
solution: String vibrates → air particles vibrate and pass it on (sound wave through the air) → eardrum vibrates → you hear it.

prompt: A river looks shallower than it really is, which can be dangerous for swimmers. Use ideas about refraction to explain why.
modelAnswer: Light from a stone on the riverbed travels up through the water and into the air towards your eye. At the water's surface the light speeds up and bends (refracts) away from the normal. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it traces the ray straight back to a point that is higher than the real stone. The bottom appears higher, so the river looks shallower than it is.

rubric.criterion: Light from the bottom travels from water into air
It changes speed and bends (refracts) at the surface
The brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so the bottom appears higher (shallower) than it really is

hints: Which way is the light travelling: into the water or out of it?
What does your brain assume about how light travels?
solution: Light from the bottom **refracts** as it leaves the water. Your brain follows the bent ray **straight back**, so the bottom seems higher. The river looks shallower than it really is.

prompt: A ray of light passes at an angle from air into a glass block. What happens to it at the surface of the glass?

options.text: It slows down and bends towards the normal
It speeds up and bends away from the normal
It slows down and bends away from the normal
It carries on in a straight line at the same speed

feedback.b: That's what happens when light comes **out** of glass into air.
feedback.c: When light slows down, it bends towards the normal, not away.
feedback.d: Light changes speed in glass. Arriving at an angle, it also changes direction.

hints: Light travels more slowly in glass than in air.
Slowing down bends the ray towards the normal.
solution: Light travels more slowly in glass, so as it enters at an angle it **slows down and bends towards the normal**. When it leaves the glass it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

prompt: Red light is shone through a **green** filter. What comes out the other side?

options.text: Almost no light, because the green filter absorbs red light
Green light
Red light
Yellow light, because red and green mix

feedback.b: A filter can't turn red light into green. It can only let through colours that are already there.
feedback.c: A green filter absorbs red light instead of letting it through.
feedback.d: The filter doesn't add green light, so there is nothing to mix.

hints: A filter only lets through (transmits) its own colour.
Is there any green light in the red beam?
solution: A green filter transmits **only green** light and absorbs other colours. The red light is absorbed, and there's no green light in it to pass through, so **almost no light** comes out.

prompt: A research ship maps the sea floor off the New Zealand coast by sending a pulse of sound straight down. The echo returns 0.4 s later. Sound travels at 1,500 m/s in sea water. How deep is the sea there?
hints: The sound goes down to the sea floor **and back up**.
Find the total distance, then halve it.
solution: Total distance: $1500 \times 0.4 = 600$ m (down and back). Depth $= 600 \div 2 = 300$ m.

The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

options.text: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
Light bends towards the normal when it slows down
Light can bend around corners by itself
Mirrors absorb light and give it out in every direction

feedback.b: That describes refraction, when light passes into a new material. Mirrors reflect light.
feedback.c: Light travels in straight lines. That's why you need mirrors to see over the wall.
feedback.d: A mirror reflects light in one predictable direction. That's why you see a clear image in it.

hints: Mirrors reflect light. Which law describes reflection?
solution: Each mirror **reflects** the light following the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal). With the mirrors at 45°, the light turns through 90° at each one.

figure.alt: A periscope: a tall tube with an opening at the top on the left and an opening at the bottom on the right. Mirror 1 at the top and mirror 2 at the bottom are parallel and tilted at 45°. A ray of light from the object travels horizontally into the top opening, reflects off mirror 1 straight down the tube, then reflects off mirror 2 horizontally out of the bottom opening into an eye. The angle between the incoming ray and mirror 1 is marked 45°, and a dashed normal is drawn at mirror 1.

modelAnswer: Light travels in straight lines, so light from the object can't bend over the wall to reach your eye. In the periscope, light from the object hits mirror 1 at the top and is reflected straight down the tube. It then hits mirror 2 at the bottom and is reflected into your eye. At each mirror the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (45°), so the light turns through 90° each time.

rubric.criterion: Light travels in straight lines, so it can't get over the wall to your eye by itself
The two mirrors reflect the light (down the tube, then into the eye), with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of reflection

hints: How does light travel?
Follow the ray in the diagram from the object to the eye.
solution: Light only travels in straight lines, so the periscope uses two reflections to change its direction: down the tube, then out into your eye.

stem: Hemi plays a note on his guitar. A microphone connected to an oscilloscope app on a tablet shows the sound as a wave trace.
prompt: Hemi tightens the string and plucks it again in the same way. The string now vibrates faster. How does the sound change?

options.text: It has a higher pitch
It is louder
It has a lower pitch
It travels faster through the air

feedback.b: Loudness depends on the amplitude (size) of the vibrations, not on how fast they are.
feedback.c: Faster vibrations mean a higher frequency, which gives a **higher** pitch.
feedback.d: All sounds travel through air at the same speed (about 340 m/s), whatever their pitch.

hints: Faster vibrations mean more vibrations per second: a higher frequency.
solution: Vibrating faster means a higher **frequency**, and a higher frequency gives a **higher pitch**.

stem: Hemi plays a note on his guitar. A microphone connected to an oscilloscope app on a tablet shows the sound as a wave trace.
prompt: Hemi plucks the string harder, without changing how tight it is. What changes?

options.text: The amplitude increases, so the sound is louder, but the pitch stays the same
The frequency increases, so the pitch is higher
The amplitude increases, so the pitch is higher
Nothing changes, because it's the same string

feedback.b: Plucking harder doesn't change how many times per second the string vibrates, so the frequency (and pitch) stay the same.
feedback.c: Amplitude controls loudness, not pitch.
feedback.d: The string vibrates with a bigger movement, which does change the sound.

hints: Plucking harder makes the string move further back and forth.
solution: Plucking harder makes bigger vibrations: a larger **amplitude**, so the sound is **louder**. The frequency, and so the pitch, stays the same, because the string's tightness and length haven't changed.

stem: Hemi plays a note on his guitar. A microphone connected to an oscilloscope app on a tablet shows the sound as a wave trace.
prompt: Trace X shows Hemi's first note. All the traces use the same oscilloscope settings. Which trace shows a sound that is **both** higher in pitch **and** louder than X?

figure.alt: Five oscilloscope traces on the same settings. Trace X (the first note) shows 3 waves across the screen with medium height. Trace A shows 3 waves that are taller. Trace B shows 6 waves at the same medium height as X. Trace C shows 6 waves that are taller. Trace D shows 2 waves that are taller.

options.text: Trace A
Trace B
Trace C
Trace D

feedback.a: Trace A has taller waves (louder), but the same number of waves as X, so it has the same pitch.
feedback.b: Trace B has more waves (higher pitch), but they are the same height as X's, so it isn't louder.
feedback.d: Trace D has taller waves (louder), but fewer waves than X, so its pitch is lower.

hints: More waves across the screen means a higher pitch. Taller waves mean a louder sound.
solution: A higher pitch means more waves squeezed across the screen (a higher frequency). Louder means taller waves (a bigger amplitude). Only **trace C** has both more waves and taller waves than X.

stem: At the school athletics day, the starter fires a starting pistol to begin the 100 m race. The pistol gives a loud bang and a puff of smoke. The timekeepers stand at the finish line, 100 m away. Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air.
prompt: Why should the timekeepers start their stopwatches when they **see** the puff of smoke, rather than when they **hear** the bang?

options.text: Light travels much faster than sound, so they see the smoke almost straight away but hear the bang later
Sound travels faster than light, so the bang arrives too early
The bang is too quiet to hear from 100 m away
Sound can't travel through the air on a windy day

feedback.b: It's the other way round: light is almost a million times faster than sound.
feedback.c: The bang is easy to hear. The problem is that it arrives a fraction of a second late.
feedback.d: Sound travels through air in any weather. Wind only changes its speed slightly.

hints: Think about why you see lightning before you hear thunder.
solution: Light travels so fast (about 300,000 km per second) that it reaches the timekeepers almost instantly. Sound takes a noticeable time to travel 100 m. Starting on the smoke means the stopwatches start when the race really starts.

stem: At the school athletics day, the starter fires a starting pistol to begin the 100 m race. The pistol gives a loud bang and a puff of smoke. The timekeepers stand at the finish line, 100 m away. Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air.
prompt: How long does the sound of the pistol take to reach the timekeepers? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
hints: Use time = distance ÷ speed.

stem: At the school athletics day, the starter fires a starting pistol to begin the 100 m race. The pistol gives a loud bang and a puff of smoke. The timekeepers stand at the finish line, 100 m away. Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air.
prompt: A timekeeper starts her stopwatch when she hears the bang, and stops it as the runner crosses the finish line. How will the time she records compare with the runner's true time?

options.text: It will be too short, by about 0.3 s
It will be too long, by about 0.3 s
It will be exactly right
It will be too long, by about 3 s

feedback.b: She starts the watch **late**, when the runner has already been running for about 0.3 s, so less time is recorded, not more.
feedback.c: Stopping the watch is fine, because the runner finishes right in front of her. The problem is the late start.
feedback.d: The delay is 100 ÷ 340, which is about 0.3 s, not 3 s. And it makes the time too short, not too long.

hints: Does she start the stopwatch before or after the race really begins?
solution: The bang reaches her about 0.29 s after the race starts, so she starts the watch late. She stops it at the right moment, so her recorded time is about **0.3 s too short**: the runner gets a faster time than they really ran.

prompt: What is the name for the bending of light as it passes from one transparent material into another, such as from air into water?

options.text: Refraction
Reflection
Absorption
Vibration

feedback.b: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface, like a mirror.
feedback.c: Absorption is when a material takes in light energy instead of letting it pass through.
feedback.d: Vibration is the back-and-forth movement that makes sound.

hints: It is why a straw looks bent in a glass of water.
solution: **Refraction** is the bending of light when it passes into a different material and changes speed.

prompt: When white light passes through a prism, it splits into a band of colours. What is this band of colours called?
hints: It is the same set of colours that you see in a rainbow, in the order ROY G BIV.
solution: It is called a **spectrum**: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

prompt: Which of these is a **luminous** object (one that gives out its own light)?

options.text: The Sun
The Moon
A mirror
A white sheet of paper

feedback.b: The Moon looks bright, but it only reflects light from the Sun.
feedback.c: A mirror reflects light very well, but it doesn't make any of its own.
feedback.d: White paper reflects all colours of light, but it gives out no light of its own.

hints: You could still see a luminous object in a completely dark room.
solution: The **Sun** is luminous: it gives out its own light. We see the Moon, mirrors and paper because they reflect light into our eyes.

prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

right.text: Lets almost all light through, e.g. clear glass
Lets some light through but scatters it, e.g. frosted glass
Lets no light through, e.g. wood
Gives out its own light, e.g. a torch

hints: 'Opaque' objects make the darkest shadows.
solution: Transparent → clear glass. Translucent → frosted glass (blurry). Opaque → no light gets through. Luminous → makes its own light.

prompt: A white object [[a]] all the colours of light that fall on it. A black object [[b]] all the colours.
hints: We see an object's colour from the light that it sends into our eyes.
solution: White objects **reflect** all colours, so all the colours reach our eyes and together they look white. Black objects **absorb** all colours, so no light is reflected to our eyes.

prompt: How are you able to see a book on your desk?

options.text: Light from a light source reflects off the book into your eyes
Light comes out of your eyes and lands on the book
The book gives out its own light
The book absorbs all the light that hits it

feedback.b: This is a very old idea, but it's wrong: our eyes **receive** light. They don't send it out.
feedback.c: Books aren't luminous. In a completely dark room you can't see them.
feedback.d: If the book absorbed all the light, none would reach your eyes and it would look black.

hints: Could you see the book in a completely dark room?
solution: Light from a source (the Sun or a lamp) **reflects** off the book, and some of the reflected light enters your eyes. That's why you can't see anything in total darkness.

prompt: When white light passes through a prism, which colour is refracted (bent) the **most**?

options.text: Violet
Red
Green
They are all bent by the same amount

feedback.b: Red is bent the **least**.
feedback.c: Green is in the middle of the spectrum, so it is bent less than violet.
feedback.d: If every colour bent by the same amount, the colours wouldn't separate into a spectrum.

hints: The colours spread out because each one bends by a different amount. Which end of ROY G BIV is furthest from red?
solution: **Violet** light is refracted the most and red the least. That is why white light spreads out into a spectrum, with red at one end and violet at the other.

prompt: On a class trip to Te Papa, Mia sees a sign with white letters in a dark gallery. The only light shining on it comes from a red spotlight. What colour do the white letters look?

options.text: Red
White
Black
Blue

feedback.b: White only looks white when all the colours shine on it. Here, only red light reaches it.
feedback.c: Black would be right if the letters absorbed red light, but a white surface reflects red light.
feedback.d: The letters can only reflect the light that reaches them, which is red.

hints: A white object reflects every colour that falls on it. Which colours are falling on it here?
solution: A white surface reflects all colours, but only **red** light is shining on it, so it reflects red light into Mia's eyes. The letters look **red**.

prompt: A ray of light hits a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 30°. What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
hints: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
Both angles are measured from the normal, one on each side of it.
solution: The angle of reflection is 30°. The two rays are on opposite sides of the normal, so the angle between them is 30° + 30° = **60°**.

prompt: Select **all** the observations that are evidence that light travels in **straight lines**.

options.text: A small torch makes shadows with clear, sharp edges
You can't see around a corner without a mirror
A laser beam shining through smoke looks perfectly straight
Sunbeams through gaps in the clouds look like straight lines
A straw in a glass of water looks bent
A prism splits white light into colours

hints: Two of these are about light changing direction as it passes into a new material.
solution: Sharp shadows, not being able to see around corners, straight laser beams and straight sunbeams all show light travelling in straight lines. The bent straw and the prism are examples of **refraction**: light changing direction as it passes into a new material.

prompt: Two astronauts are standing next to each other on the Moon, where there is no air. Explain why they use radios to talk to each other, even though they are close together.
modelAnswer: Sound is a vibration passed on from particle to particle, so it needs a medium (a solid, liquid or gas) to travel through. The Moon has no air, so the space between the astronauts is a vacuum, and the vibrations from one astronaut's voice can't travel through it to the other. Radios send radio waves, which (like light) don't need a medium and can travel through a vacuum, so radios can carry their voices.

rubric.criterion: Sound needs a medium (particles) to pass on the vibrations
The Moon has no air (a vacuum), so sound can't travel between them
Radio waves (like light) can travel through a vacuum, so radios can carry their voices

hints: What does sound need to travel through?
How is a radio signal different from a sound wave?
solution: No air means no particles to carry sound. Radio waves, like light, can cross a vacuum.

prompt: Explain how a rainbow forms when sunlight shines on raindrops.
modelAnswer: Sunlight is white light, which is a mixture of all the colours. When sunlight enters a raindrop it slows down and refracts (bends). Each colour refracts by a slightly different amount (violet the most and red the least), so the colours spread out. The light reflects off the back of the raindrop and refracts again as it comes out, spreading the colours further. We see the separated colours as a spectrum: a rainbow.

rubric.criterion: Sunlight (white light) is a mixture of all the colours
Light refracts as it enters (and leaves) the raindrops
Each colour refracts by a different amount, so the colours separate into a spectrum

hints: What is white light made of?
How does a prism split white light?
solution: Raindrops act like tiny prisms: they refract sunlight, and because each colour bends by a different amount, the colours separate into a spectrum.

prompt: A dog whistle makes a sound with a frequency of 30,000 Hz. Why can dogs hear it, but people can't?

options.text: Its frequency is above the range humans can hear (about 20 to 20,000 Hz)
The sound is too quiet for humans to hear
The sound travels too fast for human ears
Dog whistles don't make any vibrations

feedback.b: Loudness depends on amplitude. Even a loud 30,000 Hz sound can't be heard by people, because its frequency is too high.
feedback.c: All sounds travel through air at the same speed, whatever their frequency.
feedback.d: All sounds are made by vibrations. This one vibrates 30,000 times every second.

hints: Think about the range of frequencies that human ears can detect.
solution: Humans can hear frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. 30,000 Hz is above this range (it's **ultrasound**). Dogs can hear higher frequencies than people can, so they hear it.

prompt: Kahu stands between two cliffs in a narrow valley and claps once. He hears an echo from the nearer cliff after 1.0 s, and an echo from the further cliff after 3.0 s. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far apart are the two cliffs?
hints: An echo travels to the cliff **and back**, so halve the distance the sound travels.
Find Kahu's distance to each cliff, then add them together.
solution: Nearer cliff: the sound travels $340 \times 1.0 = 340$ m there and back, so the cliff is 170 m away. Further cliff: $340 \times 3.0 = 1020$ m there and back, so it is 510 m away. Kahu is between them, so the cliffs are $170 + 510 =$ **680 m** apart.

prompt: Kiri looks at a green leaf through a red filter. What colour does the leaf look?

options.text: Black
Green
Red
Yellow

feedback.b: The leaf reflects green light, but the red filter absorbs green, so no green light gets through to her eye.
feedback.c: The filter only lets red light through, but the leaf reflects hardly any red light, so there's almost no red light to pass through.
feedback.d: Light filters don't mix colours like paint. The filter removes the green light, which leaves almost nothing.

hints: Which colour of light leaves the leaf?
Which colours can get through a red filter?
solution: The green leaf reflects mainly green light. The red filter only lets red light through and absorbs green. So almost no light from the leaf reaches Kiri's eye, and the leaf looks **black** (very dark).

prompt: Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air, but at about 1,500 m/s in water. Use the particle model to explain why sound travels faster in water.
modelAnswer: Sound travels as a vibration passed from particle to particle: each vibrating particle bumps into its neighbours and makes them vibrate too. In water the particles are much closer together than in air, where they are far apart. Because the particles in water are so close, each one passes the vibration on to the next much more quickly, so the sound travels faster.

rubric.criterion: Sound is passed on by particles vibrating and bumping into their neighbours
The particles in water (a liquid) are much closer together than in air (a gas)
So the vibrations are passed on more quickly, and sound travels faster in water

hints: How do vibrations get from one particle to the next?
Compare how far apart the particles are in a liquid and in a gas.
solution: Closer particles pass the vibrations on more quickly, so sound travels faster in liquids than in gases (and faster still in most solids).
